pron_note: The verb is ar-TIK-yuh-LAYT — same spelling, different ending: the adjective mumbles the last syllable, the verb sounds it out.
means:
**Adj.:** fluent and clear in speech — able to say exactly what you mean.
**Verb:** to put something into clear words, especially something that was previously vague; also, literally, **to join by a hinge**.

The idea underneath is *jointedness*, not eloquence. To **articulate** a fear is to break a shapeless dread into named parts; an **articulate** speaker isn't just smooth, they deliver thought in distinct, well-hinged pieces you can follow. That's why bones and lorries articulate too — they're jointed so they can bend.

One register warning: as praise for a person, it can land as a backhanded compliment when the speaker is implying they didn't expect fluency.
trick_line: An **articulated** lorry is one long thing split at a **joint** — an articulate speaker splits one long thought the same way.
trick_unpack: Both senses are the same act: putting joints into something so it can move and be followed.
sentences: The witness proved unexpectedly **articulate**, laying out a decade of grievance in three clean paragraphs.
I couldn't **articulate** why the flat felt wrong — it just did.
in_the_wild: The **articulated** lorry (and the bendy bus) — the bit in the middle that hinges is the articulation. Same word, visible joint.
etymology: Latin **articulus** = *"little joint"* (from **artus**, joint). Hence **article** — originally a distinct joint or clause of a text, which is why treaties have articles. Greek cousin **arthron** gives you **arthritis**, the disease of the joints.
one_line: Clear-speaking; to put a vague thought into distinct words.
